title: 2 Chronicles 14:1–8
context: After Abijah’s death, Asa reigns and the land is quiet for ten years. Asa does what is good and right: he removes foreign altars, high places, pillars, and Asherah poles, and commands Judah to seek the LORD and keep His law. He fortifies cities during the years of rest, telling the people that the LORD has given rest because they have sought Him. He also has a large army from Judah and Benjamin. The parallel is 1 Kings 15:9–15. Kings says the high places were not taken away (1 Kings 15:14), and Chronicles itself says so later (15:17), while 14:3 and 14:5 say Asa removed them; these statements are named here rather than harmonized.

verses.text: So Abijah slept with his fathers, and they buried him in David’s city; and Asa his son reigned in his place. In his days, the land was quiet ten years.
verses.arminianNotes: Abijah dies, Asa reigns, and the land is quiet ten years. Arminian readers note that the Chronicler links peace with faithfulness, a theme developed throughout Asa’s reign.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the quiet years as God’s gift of rest. Both traditions note that 1 Kings 15:16 speaks of war between Asa and Baasha all their days; the difference is named without being resolved.

verses.text: Asa did that which was good and right in the LORD his God’s eyes,
verses.arminianNotes: Asa does what is good and right in the LORD’s eyes. Arminian readers see a king who chooses faithfulness, beginning his reign with reform rather than continuing his predecessors’ compromises.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s favor at work in Asa’s good beginning. Shared ground: the verdict parallels 1 Kings 15:11, which adds “as David his father did,” and both traditions read it as a positive assessment.

verses.text: for he took away the foreign altars and the high places, broke down the pillars, cut down the Asherah poles,
verses.arminianNotes: Asa removes foreign altars and high places, breaks pillars, and cuts down Asherah poles. Arminian readers note the energy of the reform, aimed at the objects of false worship throughout the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 15:17 and 1 Kings 15:14 say the high places were not taken away; the statements are named, not harmonized. Both traditions read the verse as describing a serious effort at reform.

verses.text: and commanded Judah to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, and to obey his law and command.
verses.arminianNotes: Asa commands Judah to seek the LORD and obey His law. Arminian readers note that “seek” is a key word for the Chronicler, describing wholehearted turning to God that Asa calls the people to make.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the king leading the people in covenant faithfulness. Shared ground: both traditions read the command as a call to worship and obedience, the theme that will shape the rest of Asa’s story.

verses.text: Also he took away out of all the cities of Judah the high places and the sun images; and the kingdom was quiet before him.
verses.arminianNotes: Asa removes high places and sun images from Judah’s cities, and the kingdom is quiet before him. Arminian readers note the link between reform and rest that the Chronicler draws again here.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see rest as God’s gift, not as a reward earned by reform. Both traditions note again that 15:17 says the high places were not taken away out of Israel, a difference the notes name without resolving.

verses.text: He built fortified cities in Judah; for the land was quiet, and he had no war in those years, because the LORD had given him rest.
verses.arminianNotes: Asa builds fortified cities during the quiet years, because the LORD has given him rest. Arminian readers see wise use of peace, preparing for future challenges while circumstances allow.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers notice the reason given at the end of the verse: the LORD had granted rest. Building walls and trusting God are not set against each other here, a point neither tradition disputes.

verses.text: For he said to Judah, “Let’s build these cities and make walls around them, with towers, gates, and bars. The land is yet before us, because we have sought the LORD our God. We have sought him, and he has given us rest on every side.” So they built and prospered.
verses.arminianNotes: Asa urges Judah to build because they have sought the LORD and He has given rest. Arminian readers note the clear connection Asa draws between seeking God and receiving rest on every side.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see seeking God as the response His grace produces, with rest as His gift. Both traditions agree that the verse ties seeking and rest together, and they read it within the Chronicler’s theology of blessing.

verses.text: Asa had an army of three hundred thousand out of Judah who bore bucklers and spears, and two hundred eighty thousand out of Benjamin who bore shields and drew bows. All these were mighty men of valor.
verses.arminianNotes: Asa has three hundred thousand from Judah and two hundred eighty thousand from Benjamin. Arminian readers note that the figures are large and read in more than one way, as with other numbers in Chronicles.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Judah’s spearmen and Benjamin’s archers are listed separately, reflecting different weapons and roles. The totals are reported as written, and these notes do not try to reconcile them with other data.
